title: Broken Memories: Detecting and Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models with Degraded Generations

paper.title: Broken Memories : Detecting and Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models with Degraded Generations
paper.abstract:
Abstract. While diffusion models excel at generating high-quality images, their tendency to memorize training data poses significant privacy and copyright risks.
In this work, we for the first time identify that memorization induces internal numerical instability, often manifesting as visually “broken” artifacts.
Inspired by stability analysis in numerical methods, we introduce empirical stability regions based on latent update norms to quantitatively characterize stable behavior during generation.
Leveraging this, we propose a principled, on-the-fly framework for step-wise detection and adaptive mitigation.
Our approach suppresses memorization without altering prompts or guidance, thereby preserving semantic fidelity and image quality.
Extensive experiments on Stable Diffusion 1.4 demonstrate that our method achieves an AUC > 0.999 >0.999 detection performance and a 0.0 % 0.0\% memorization rate after mitigation with negligible overhead ( ≈ 0.01 \approx 0.01 s per image).

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Recent advancements in diffusion models have led to breakthroughs in high-quality image generation, showcasing immense potential in creative arts ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . However, as model scales and training data volumes continue to grow, diffusion models increasingly face a critical issue: memorized generation ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) . It is evident from recent research that diffusion models inadvertently replicate or highly resemble specific images from their training datasets, leading to potential privacy leakage and copyright infringements ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1. Memorized generations (blue and orange borders, using PNDM and DDIM) show clear degradation—such as broken details or abnormal intermediate results—compared to non-memorized generations (green border). The yellow shaded regions in both plots indicate the empirical stability regions for latent norm ( ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| ) and latent update norm ( ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| ). Memorized samples consistently deviate from these stability regions during generation, while non-memorized samples stay within them. This motivates our approach: by monitoring and intervening these latent deviations, we can accurately detect and mitigate memorization on the fly. Existing research has investigated memorization from multiple perspectives. Early studies detect it by comparing generated images with training samples ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) . Later works analyze the internal mechanisms underlying memorization, such as attention weights ( Ren et al., 2024 ) or magnitude of conditional guidance directions ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) . To mitigate memorization, these methods propose interventions like modifying prompts ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) , tuning text embeddings ( Wen et al., 2024 ) , initial latents ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) , or directly adjusting guidance scale ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . However, these approaches generally face two major limitations: • Dependence on re-generation: Most existing inference-time methods operate on a detect-then-retry basis. They cannot correct the trajectory seamlessly. Instead, detection triggers an abort, requiring the generation to be restarted with modified inputs, which increases latency and computational cost. • Heuristic or static interventions: Mitigation typically relies on fixed rules or static adjustments to prompts, embeddings, or guidance scales, which compromise semantic fidelity and fail to adapt to the dynamic nature of memorization, leading to over- or under-mitigation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a principled framework for on-the-fly detection and adaptive mitigation of memorization in diffusion models, based on the modeling of empirical stability regions of the generation dynamics. Our method is inspired by a key observation: when generating memorized samples, the PNDM (Pseudo-Numerical methods for Diffusion Models) scheduler ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , i.e., the default scheduler of Stable Diffusion v1 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , often produces noticeable visual degradation, such as a “broken” appearance, while non-memorized prompts yield normal generations (see Fig. 1 ). We trace this phenomenon to a fundamental cause: memorization manifests as numerical instability in the latent dynamics . Specifically, we observe that memorization causes anomalous deviations in the latent update per step ( δ t \delta_{t} ) from model’s empirical stable region , which can be estimated from the model’s normal behavior. We further prove that for non-memorized prompts, δ t \delta_{t} remains within this stability region, while for memorized prompts, it exhibits large, erratic fluctuations that lead to unstable denoising trajectories and visible artifacts in generated images. Notably, such instability is not limited to PNDM: with non-numerical schedulers like DDIM ( Song et al., 2022 ) , even when the generated images appear visually plausible, we still observe similar anomalies throughout the generation in the internal latent space. Building on this insight, we propose a high-precision, step-wise detection system that monitors the deviation of δ t \delta_{t} from the empirical stability region at each denoising step. This enables accurate diagnosis of whether the current generation trajectory is tending toward memorization. Detected instabilities trigger an adaptive mitigation strategy that distinguishes between mild and strong memorization: mild cases are regularized early through latent-magnitude constraints, while strong cases require stricter joint constraints on both latent and update norms throughout the trajectory. Both mitigations are performed based on the estimated stability regions from a small set of normal prompts (e.g., 50 50 generations from LAION-400M ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) ). The entire process operates on the fly , with no modification to the prompt or guidance, ensuring both semantic fidelity and image quality. Table 1 summarizes representative baseline methods, highlighting that our method uniquely achieves all three capabilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We present the first systematic analysis linking degraded memorization generation to numerical instability in diffusion sampling, revealing distinctive anomalies in latent updates ( δ t \delta_{t} ) magnitudes. • We introduce the concept of empirical stability regions , grounded in numerical stability theory and extended to broader scenarios, to characterize and diagnose normal versus memorized generation in diffusion models. • We develop an on-the-fly, diagnosis-driven framework that adaptively constrains the generation trajectories only when instability is detected, surpassing existing heuristic or static methods. • Our approach achieves superior detection accuracy (AUC > 0.999 >0.999 ) in identifying memorization and completely eliminates memorized generations ( 0.0 % 0.0\% rate) while preserving high image quality and semantic fidelity, with minimal overhead ( ≈ 0.01 \approx 0.01 s per image). sections.heading: 2.1. Memorization Detection in Diffusion Models
sections.text: Recent studies have revealed that diffusion models are prone to memorizing and reproducing training images ( Chavhan et al., 2024 ; Bonnaire et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Guan et al., 2025 ) . Early detection methods rely on post-hoc comparisons between generated samples and the training set, such as using Euclidean distance ( Carlini et al., 2023 ) or features extracted by self-supervised copy detection (SSCD) models ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ) . However, these image-level approaches are often confounded by complex patterns and require the generation to be fully completed. To enable earlier detection, subsequent works have explored internal model signals. Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) and Ren et al. ( Ren et al., 2024 ) demonstrated that memorized prompts induce significantly larger guidance magnitudes and distinct attention patterns compared to non-memorized ones. Beyond signal magnitude, recent studies have emphasized the dynamics and geometry of the generative process. Brokman et al. ( Brokman et al., 2025 ) analyzed the memorization geometry via the mean-curvature of the CFG vector field, while Jeon et al. ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) linked memorization to the sharpness of the initial latent probability landscape. These works provide a deeper theoretical understanding of why memorization manifests as anomalous dynamics. Other approaches focus on specific scenarios, such as detecting memorized generations with particular images ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) or identifying local memorization patterns ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . Despite these advances, most detection methods generally serve as diagnostic tools rather than real-time controllers. Even when used for mitigation, they typically trigger a re-generation rather than enabling seamless, on-the-fly intervention during the generation trajectory.

sections.heading: 2.2. Memorization Mitigation in Diffusion Models
sections.text: Mitigation strategies can be broadly categorized into training-time and test-time interventions. Training-time methods generally introduce regularization or data filtering to reduce memorization risk. Common approaches include monitoring guidance magnitude ( Wen et al., 2024 ) or attention patterns ( Ren et al., 2024 ) during training, and removing batches that exceed predefined thresholds. Other methods augment prompts to reduce replication likelihood ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) . While effective, these techniques require model retraining or fine-tuning, which is computationally prohibitive for large-scale models and inflexible for deployed systems. Test-time approaches, on the other hand, aim to mitigate memorization during the inference phase. Typical methods involve modifying prompts ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) , optimizing text embeddings ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , optimizing initial latents ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) , adjusting attention weights ( Ren et al., 2024 ) , or tuning guidance scales ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . However, these strategies face two critical limitations. First, they often operate on a detect-then-retry paradigm: mitigation is applied only after a problematic generation is detected partially or fully, triggering a restart with modified inputs. This dependency on regeneration significantly increases inference latency. Second, interventions are typically applied as heuristic or static adjustments, e.g., fixed guidance reduction or embedding optimization at initial step, rather than adapting dynamically to the evolving generation trajectory. This can lead to either under-mitigation or over-constraint, potentially harming image quality. In contrast, our work introduces an adaptive, trajectory-aware framework that enables on-the-fly monitoring and seamless intervention without the need for regeneration, effectively ensuring both safety and efficiency.

sections.heading: 3.3. Schedulers
sections.text: Schedulers play a crucial role in diffusion models by controlling the denoising trajectory during the sampling process, determining how the model transitions from pure noise to a clean sample. Denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIM) ( Song et al., 2022 ) introduce a non-stochastic, deterministic alternative to sampling. The DDIM update at step t − 1 t-1 is given by: (3) 𝐳 t − 1 = α ¯ t − 1 ​ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) + 1 − α ¯ t − 1 ​ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) , \mathbf{z}_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c), where 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) = 1 α ¯ t ​ ( 𝐳 t − 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)\right) denotes the model’s estimate of the original clean sample at the current step. This formulation corresponds to solving an ODE defined by the probability flow of the diffusion process. Pseudo numerical methods for diffusion models (PNDM) ( Liu et al., 2022 ) accelerate DDIM by using high-order numerical solvers to integrate the underlying ODE. Given the DDIM update as an Euler discretization, PNDM improves sampling efficiency and quality via higher-order methods such as Runge–Kutta ( Butcher, 1996 ) or Adams-Bashforth schemes ( Durran, 1991 ) . The fourth-order Adams-Bashforth (AB4) method used by PNDM is defined as: (4) 𝐳 t + 1 = 𝐳 t + Δ ​ t ⋅ ∑ i = 0 3 b i ​ f θ ​ ( 𝐳 t − i , t − i , c ) , \mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\mathbf{z}_{t}+\Delta t\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{3}b_{i}f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t-i},t-i,c), where b i b_{i} are fixed coefficients derived from the method, Δ ​ t \Delta t is the integration step size, and f θ ​ ( 𝐳 , t , c ) = − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 , t , c ) f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},t,c)=-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},t,c) represents the model’s denoising prediction. 1 1 1 Following the convention of numerical ODE solvers, the equation is written in the forward direction ( t → t + 1 t\to t+1 ), while the actual sampling process proceeds in the reverse direction ( t → t − 1 t\to t-1 ), i.e., from noise to data. The formulation bridges the gap between the deep generative model and classical ODE solvers by viewing the denoising trajectory as an integration path over estimated derivatives.

sections.heading: 4.3. Extending Stability Analysis to Reconstructed Initial Latent
sections.text: Having attributed the visual degradation in PNDM to numerical instability, we now broaden our scope to the widely-used DDIM sampler ( Song et al., 2022 ) . We demonstrate that deviating from the stability region is a universal signature of memorization: even when DDIM produces visually clean images, its underlying latent trajectory still significantly diverges from the stable manifold. To examine whether instability persists, we turn to the reconstruction mechanism of DDIM. At each timestep t t , DDIM performs deterministic recovery of an estimate of the initial latent 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} via: 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) = 1 α ¯ t ​ ( 𝐳 t − 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) ) . \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)\right). This quantity is meant to approximate the actual z 0 z_{0} at current timestep t t , i.e., the latent that would be decoded by the autoencoder into the final image x 0 x_{0} . As such, it acts as an intermediate “anchor” that encapsulates the accumulated influence of all denoising steps up to time t t . sections.heading: 5.1. Detection via Instable Latent Updates
sections.text: Based on the empirical stability region in Def. 1 , we can detect memorization artifacts by monitoring deviations from the region during generation. At each denoising step t t , we compute the absolute Z-score of the latent update norm: s t = | ‖ δ t ‖ − μ t σ t | . s_{t}=\left|\frac{\|\delta_{t}\|-\mu_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\right|. A high s t s_{t} indicates an anomalous update, suggesting potential memorization. We summarize a sample’s trajectory by the maximum absolute Z-score over the first s s steps 2 2 2 Note that taking the maximum Z-score across s s steps introduces a multiple testing problem, which results in an expected log ⁡ s \sqrt{\log s} shift in S mem S_{\text{mem}} in our multi-step detection scenario. However, since this systemetic shift applies to both memorized and normal samples, it does not affect the relative detection performance. : S mem = max 1 ≤ t ≤ s ⁡ s t . S_{\text{mem}}=\max_{1\leq t\leq s}s_{t}. This approach efficiently highlights sharp deviations from normal behavior and is applicable to any diffusion sampler. Notably, high-order solvers like PNDM further amplify such anomalies, enhancing detection sensitivity. Crucially, rather than serving merely as a post-hoc scoring tool for filtering memorized generations, this dynamically calibrated step-wise metric s t s_{t} is intrinsically designed to act as a real-time monitor. The true value of this diagnostic signal lies in its ability to pinpoint the exact moment of instability, which serves as the fundamental prerequisite for our on-the-fly mitigation strategy.

sections.text: While monitoring s t s_{t} effectively flags potential memorization, tailoring the mitigation intensity requires gauging the severity of the instability. To this end, we incorporate the reconstructed initial latent 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} as a semantic stability proxy, allowing us to differentiate between mild and strong memorization artifacts. We thus propose a two-level adaptive mitigation strategy. To facilitate this, we define an additional empirical stability region ℛ z ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{z}^{(t)} for the latent norm ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| , analogous to ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} in Def. 1 . Based on the magnitude of s 0 ( t ∗ ) s_{0}^{(t^{*})} , we apply the following specific interventions: 1. Mild Memorization ( τ mild < s 0 ( t ∗ ) ≤ τ strong \tau_{\text{mild}}<s_{0}^{(t^{*})}\leq\tau_{\text{strong}} ): • For the first k k steps, if both s t s_{t} and s 0 ( t ) s_{0}^{(t)} exceed τ mild \tau_{\text{mild}} , and s 0 ( t ) ≤ τ strong s_{0}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{\text{strong}} , we rescale 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)} to the empirical mean μ 0 ( t ) \mu_{0}^{(t)} . • Throughout the trajectory, we constrain ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| to remain within ℛ z ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{z}^{(t)} only when ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| exceeds ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} . 2. sections.heading: 5.3. Advantages over Prior Work
sections.text: Our framework enables on-the-fly trajectory correction , fundamentally distinguishing it from prior inference-time approaches. While existing methods ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) can potentially detect memorization at early steps (e.g., via prediction magnitude), their mitigation paradigms remain distinctively costly. Specifically, once memorization is flagged, these methods typically require aborting the current process and applying iterative optimization on prompts or embeddings, followed by a complete restart of the generation. Even if detection happens at step t = 1 t=1 , the overhead of computing gradients for optimization and restarting the sampling loop is non-negligible. In contrast, our approach acts as a streaming filter : our detection mechanism enables instability monitoring at each step, and our mitigation strategy applies instantaneous projection to pull the latent state back into the stability region as soon as instability is detected, without interrupting the diffusion process. This allows the generation to proceed seamlessly, enforcing safety constraints with virtually zero additional latency compared to standard inference. Beyond computational efficiency, our framework offers a theoretical advantage: by grounding detection in numerical stability rather than heuristic magnitude thresholds, it provides a principled explanation for why memorization leads to broken generations, unifying prior observations under a consistent dynamical perspective.

sections.heading: 6.1. Memorization Detection
sections.text: Datasets and Models. Three datasets are used in this experiment, i.e., one memorized and two non-memorized. Following prior works, the memorized set contains 500 500 prompts corresponding to known duplicated images in the LAION dataset ( Schuhmann et al., 2021 ; Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) constructed by ( Webster, 2023 ) , which includes both exact and template verbatim samples. For non-memorized sets, the one used for evaluation contains a total of 500 500 prompts sampled from the Lexica.art gallery, the COCO-2017 validation set caption, and generated by GPT-4 ( Achiam et al., 2023 ) following the construction in ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . Another non-memorized set is used for estimating the empirical stability region, which contains 50 50 prompts sampled from the LAION-400M ( Schuhmann et al., 2021 ) dataset. For detection, we consider pretrained SD 1.4, 1.5, 2.1, with PNDM ( Liu et al., 2022 ) and DDIM ( Song et al., 2022 ) . For SD 1.5, 2.1 results, please refer to Appendix E.3 . Metrics. Following prior works ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) , we use two standard metrics, Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) and True Positive Rate at 1 % 1\% False Positive Rate (TPR@ 1 % 1\% FPR). Baselines. We consider three representative baselines. Ren et al. ( Ren et al., 2024 ) uses the entropy of cross-attention maps as a signal, i.e., memorized prompts lead to more stable entropy. Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) computes the L2 norm of the guidance ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( z t , t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( z t , t , ϕ ) ‖ 2 ||\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t,\phi)||_{2} . Jeon et al. ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) extends Wen et al.’s approach by incorporating the Hessian of the guidance to account for the local curvature. Results. As shown in Table 2 , our method, which monitors the Z-score of the latent update norm, consistently outperforms existing baselines in the vast majority of settings, achieving high AUC and TPR@ 1 % 1\% FPR, demonstrating its superior accuracy and reliability. Such accurate per-step detection performance is crucial for mitigation. We also show in Appendix E.2 that our method is insensitive to the distribution and size of the reference set. The amplifying effect of PNDM. While our method already yields high detection accuracy with standard schedulers like DDIM, PNDM can further enhance the signal contrast. Due to its multi-step nature, PNDM accumulates the instability inherent to memorized prompts, thereby boosting the performance of methods sensitive to guidance dynamics, as shown in Table 3 . In contrast, Ren et al. does not benefit from this, as its attention-entropy-based indicator is relatively independent of the solver’s integration trajectory. Figure 3. sections.heading: 6.2. Memorization Mitigation
sections.text: Datasets and Models. We evaluate mitigation on two scenarios using the DDIM scheduler ( Song et al., 2022 ) : pretrained SD 1.4 (using the same datasets as detection) and SD 1.4 finetuned on a LAION subset to simulate memorization ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . For practical evaluation, all online mitigation thresholds are calibrated to 1 % 1\% FPR on the LAION-400M reference set. Due to space constraints, results for the finetuned SD are detailed in Appendix E.4 . Metrics. We use Self-Supervised Copy Detection (SSCD) ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ) to detect whether the generated image is a memorized one, which measures the embedding similarity of two images with an SSL model. The memorization rate (Mem Rate) evaluates the portion of memorized images generated with SSCD > 0.5 >0.5 . CLIP Score ( Hessel et al., 2022 ; Radford et al., 2021 ) on both memorized and non-memorized sets is used to measure the semantic alignment between the generated image and the prompt. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2018 ) is used to evaluate the overall quality and realism of the generated images. More details can be found in Appendix D.3 . Baselines. We consider five mitigation baselines. Among them, Random Tokens Addition (RTA) ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) mitigates memorization by randomly adding tokens to the original input. Ren et al. ( Ren et al., 2024 ) suppresses attention weights corresponding to tokens that trigger memorization. Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) performs optimization on the prompt embedding to steer it away from memorized regions in the embedding space. Jeon et al. ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) enhances Wen et al.’s method by considering the local curvature while optimizing the initial latent. Jain et al. ( Jain et al., 2025 ) introduces a dynamic guidance scale that pushes the generation trajectory away from memorized content, particularly in the early steps. As summarized in Table 1 , our method is the only one that adaptively mitigates memorization on the fly with detection. Quantitative Results. Fig. 3 visualizes the trade-off between Mem Rate and FID. Detailed results are in Appendix E.4 . Most baselines fail to reach the Pareto optimal region. Optimization-based methods (Wen et al., Jeon et al.) cluster in the top region with high Mem Rates, as their initial-step mitigation is insufficient to prevent memorization from resurfacing. Conversely, heuristic methods (RTA and Ren et al.), while reducing Mem Rate further, drift significantly towards the high-FID region (right side), since their coarse-grained interventions disrupt memorization at the cost of degrading quality. In contrast, our method dominates the bottom-left Pareto front, achieving a 0 0 Mem Rate with the lowest FID. Overall, we observe a positive correlation where mitigation improves quality. This reflects that memorization is essentially a form of mode collapse. Our adaptive mitigation not only eradicates duplicates on-the-fly with negligible computational overhead ( ≈ 0.01 \approx 0.01 s/img, see Table 4 ), but also restores diverse generation, thereby improving fidelity. Visualizations. Quantitative metrics alone can be deceptive. First, high CLIP Scores often mask mitigation failures by rewarding the high-quality generation of memorized replicas. Second, a low Mem Rate does not guarantee success, as it may simply reflect the generation of unrelated content (over-mitigation), characterized by a drastic drop in CLIP Score. Therefore, visual inspection in Fig. 4 is essential. The results reveal two main failure modes in baselines: either retaining memorized content (most baselines) or suffering from excessive semantic deviation (Jain et al.). Our method strikes the optimal balance, effectively eliminating memorized content while preserving high semantic fidelity. Figure 5. Ablation study of ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| and ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| constraints. Ablation Study on Stability Constraints. We further analyze the effect of different stability constraints on mitigating memorization, as shown in Fig. 5 . Three types of constraints are considered in our mitigation: the reconstructed latent norm ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| , the latent norm ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| , and the latent update norm ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| . The ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| constraint is consistently applied as a baseline for stabilizing intermediate reconstructions in both mild and strong memorization cases. For mild memorization, adding the ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| constraint effectively removes memorized content while preserving visual quality. However, when jointly enforcing both ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| and ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| , the generation quality significantly deteriorates, and traces of memorization even reappear. This is possibly due to over-constrained dynamics that disrupt the denoising trajectory. For strong memorization, applying only the ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| constraint is insufficient, as it tends to preserve structural patterns of the memorized image and results in poor image quality. In contrast, jointly enforcing both ‖ 𝐳 t ‖ \|\mathbf{z}_{t}\| and ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| constraints successfully removes memorization and restores high-quality outputs. These observations highlight the importance of adaptively selecting constraint combinations based on the severity of memorization. Our multi-constraint design enables effective mitigation across different scenarios. Case Study. Fig. 6 underscores the necessity of on-the-fly mitigation. Static methods like RTA and Wen et al. apply constraints only at the initialization stage (via token addition or embedding optimization). As the visualization reveals, these early constraints often fail to persist, allowing the denoising trajectory to drift back towards memorized attractors in subsequent steps. In contrast, our framework monitors the process in real-time and actively intercepts these drifts, adaptively mitigating whenever memorization signals resurface to ensure a unique generation. sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we uncovered a fundamental link between memorization and numerical instability in diffusion models. By analyzing the latent dynamics, we showed that memorized prompts drive the generation trajectory out of the empirical stability regions characteristic of normal samples, which is a phenomenon unified across different samplers (e.g., PNDM and DDIM). Guided by this theoretical insight, we proposed a real-time framework for memorization detection and mitigation. Our method monitors stability deviations step-by-step and applies adaptive trajectory corrections on the fly, eliminating the need for costly re-generation. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach not only achieves superior detection accuracy and complete memorization suppression but also preserves image quality with negligible computational overhead. We believe this stability-centric perspective offers a new, principled direction for building trustworthy generative models.

sections.heading: Appendix A Detailed Proofs
sections.text: In this section, we provide detailed proofs for Theorem 2 and 5 presented in the main text. Theorem 1 (Normal Trajectories Stability). Let δ t \delta_{t} denote the latent updates of normal prompts, and let ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} be the empirical stability region defined in Def. 1 . Then with high probability, we have: ‖ δ t ‖ ∈ ℛ δ ( t ) , ∀ t ∈ { 1 , … , T } . \|\delta_{t}\|\in\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)},\quad\forall t\in\{1,\dots,T\}. In other words, latent trajectories from non-memorized prompts tend to stay within their corresponding empirical stability region throughout the generation. Sketch. The empirical region ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} is constructed from the empirical mean μ t \mu_{t} and std. σ t \sigma_{t} over ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| sampled from the training set. Under the assumption that these updates follow a sub-Gaussian distribution ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) , concentration bounds ensure that most values lie within [ μ t ± γ ​ σ t ] [\mu_{t}\pm\gamma\sigma_{t}] . Thus, the definition of ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} captures the high-probability support of normal trajectories. ∎ Proof. Let δ t := 𝐳 t − 𝐳 t + 1 \delta_{t}:=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}_{t+1} denote the latent update at step t t for a normal prompt. By the formulation of diffusion sampling, the update δ t \delta_{t} is determined by the denoising network f θ f_{\theta} and the scheduler (e.g., PNDM, DDIM, taking one-step Euler method as an example here for simplicity): 𝐳 t + 1 = 𝐳 t − Δ ​ t ⋅ f θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) \mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\Delta t\cdot f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) ⇒ δ t = 𝐳 t − 𝐳 t + 1 = Δ ​ t ⋅ f θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) . \Rightarrow\delta_{t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\Delta t\cdot f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c). For normal prompts, the output of f θ f_{\theta} is governed by the learned distribution of the training data and is assumed to be sub-Gaussian ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) . That is, for each t t , the random variable ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| satisfies the sub-Gaussian tail bound: ℙ ⁡ ( | ‖ δ t ‖ − μ t | ≥ γ ​ σ t ) ≤ 2 ​ exp ⁡ ( − γ 2 2 ) , \mathbb{P}\left(|\|\delta_{t}\|-\mu_{t}|\geq\gamma\sigma_{t}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2}\right), where μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} are the empirical mean and standard deviation of ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| over normal prompts at step t t , and γ \gamma is a positive constant. Therefore, for a sufficiently large γ \gamma (e.g., γ = 3 \gamma=3 ), the probability that ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| falls outside the interval [ μ t − γ ​ σ t , μ t + γ ​ σ t ] [\mu_{t}-\gamma\sigma_{t},\,\mu_{t}+\gamma\sigma_{t}] is exponentially small. By the union bound over all T T steps, the probability that any ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| deviates from ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} is at most 2 T exp ( − γ 2 / 2 ) 2T\exp(-\gamma^{2}/2) , which remains small for moderate T T and γ \gamma . Thus, with high probability, for all t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , ‖ δ t ‖ ∈ ℛ δ ( t ) = [ μ t − γ ​ σ t , μ t + γ ​ σ t ] \|\delta_{t}\|\in\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)}=[\mu_{t}-\gamma\sigma_{t},\,\mu_{t}+\gamma\sigma_{t}] as claimed. This completes the proof that latent trajectories from non-memorized prompts tend to stay within their corresponding empirical stability region throughout the generation process. ∎ Remark on PNDM and Multi-Step Solvers: The above proof is based on the single-step update formulation. In practice, multi-step solvers such as PNDM (AB4) ( Liu et al., 2022 ) compute the latent update δ t \delta_{t} as a weighted combination of denoising predictions from several previous steps: δ t = Δ ​ t ⋅ ∑ i = 0 3 b i ​ f θ ​ ( 𝐳 t − i , t − i , c ) \delta_{t}=\Delta t\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{3}b_{i}f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t-i},t-i,c) This "transfer part" introduces momentum and extrapolation effects, which can amplify local irregularities in the latent trajectory. However, as long as the denoising outputs f θ f_{\theta} for normal prompts remain sub-Gaussian and bounded, the resulting δ t \delta_{t} still concentrates within the empirical stability region ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} with high probability. For memorized prompts, the multi-step combination may further exaggerate deviations, making instability more detectable. Proposition 2 (Instability of Memorized Trajectories). Let c m ​ e ​ m c_{mem} be a memorized prompt where the conditional noise prediction norm significantly dominates the unconditional one, such that ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ ≥ β ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|\geq\beta\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\| for a large factor β > 1 \beta>1 . With guidance scale w w , the magnitude of the latent update ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| for the memorized prompt satisfies: ‖ δ t ‖ m ​ e ​ m ≈ w ⋅ C ⋅ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ , \|\delta_{t}\|_{mem}\approx w\cdot C\cdot\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|, where C C is a constant related to the step size. Consequently, due to the excessively large gradient norm ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\| (large β \beta ), the resulting update ‖ δ t ‖ m ​ e ​ m \|\delta_{t}\|_{mem} exceeds the upper bound of the stability region ℛ δ ( t ) = [ μ t ± γ ​ σ t ] \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)}=[\mu_{t}\pm\gamma\sigma_{t}] calibrated on normal samples, causing the trajectory to diverge from the stable manifold. Proof. By definition of classifier-free guidance (CFG), the final noise prediction ϵ θ CFG \epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}} is given by: ϵ θ CFG ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) = ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) + w ⋅ ( ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ) . \epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)=\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)+w\cdot\left(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\right). Rearranging terms, we can express it as a weighted sum: ϵ θ CFG ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) = w ⋅ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) + ( 1 − w ) ⋅ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) . \epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)=w\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)+(1-w)\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi). Now, we consider the magnitude of this vector. Using the triangle inequality properties ( | ‖ a ‖ − ‖ b ‖ | ≤ ‖ a − b ‖ |\|a\|-\|b\||\leq\|a-b\| ), we can bound the norm from below: ‖ ϵ θ CFG ‖ \displaystyle\|\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}\| = ‖ w ⋅ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) − ( w − 1 ) ⋅ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ‖ \displaystyle=\|w\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)-(w-1)\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\| ≥ w ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) ‖ − ( w − 1 ) ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ‖ , \displaystyle\geq w\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)\|-(w-1)\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\|, assuming w > 1 w>1 . We invoke the memorization assumption: for a memorized prompt c m ​ e ​ m c_{mem} , the model is overfitted, resulting in gradients (noise predictions) that are significantly sharper than the unconditional priors. Specifically, we assume ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ ≥ β ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|\geq\beta\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\| for some large factor β > 1 \beta>1 . Substituting ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , ϕ ) ‖ ≤ 1 β ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi)\|\leq\frac{1}{\beta}\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\| into the lower bound: ‖ ϵ θ CFG ‖ \displaystyle\|\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}\| ≥ w ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ − ( w − 1 ) ​ 1 β ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ \displaystyle\geq w\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|-(w-1)\frac{1}{\beta}\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\| = ( w − w − 1 β ) ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ . \displaystyle=\left(w-\frac{w-1}{\beta}\right)\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|. For memorization, β \beta is large (i.e., the conditional signal overwhelmingly dominates the unconditional noise). As β → ∞ \beta\to\infty , the term w − 1 β → 0 \frac{w-1}{\beta}\to 0 , leading to the approximation: ‖ ϵ θ CFG ‖ ≈ w ​ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ . \|\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}\|\approx w\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|. Next, relating this to the latent update δ t \delta_{t} . For a generic solver step, the update is proportional to the noise prediction: δ t = 𝐳 t − 𝐳 t + 1 = Δ ​ t ⋅ ϵ θ CFG . \delta_{t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\Delta t\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}. Thus, the magnitude ‖ δ t ‖ \|\delta_{t}\| is: ‖ δ t ‖ m ​ e ​ m = Δ ​ t ⋅ ‖ ϵ θ CFG ‖ ≈ Δ ​ t ⋅ w ⋅ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ . \|\delta_{t}\|_{mem}=\Delta t\cdot\|\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}\|\approx\Delta t\cdot w\cdot\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|. Note that for multi-step solvers like PNDM, δ t \delta_{t} is a linear combination of past ϵ \epsilon ’s, but the dominant term is still proportional to the current scale, so we use a constant C C in the proposition statement to subsume Δ ​ t \Delta t and solver coefficients. Finally, we consider the stability region ℛ δ ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{(t)} . Its upper bound, B m ​ a ​ x = μ t + γ ​ σ t B_{max}=\mu_{t}+\gamma\sigma_{t} , is determined by the statistics of normal prompts. For normal prompts, the conditional gradient ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c n ​ o ​ r ​ m ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{norm})\| is bounded, resulting in a stable reference distribution for δ t \delta_{t} . In contrast, for memorized prompts, the overfitting leads to an intrinsically much larger gradient norm: ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c m ​ e ​ m ) ‖ ≫ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c n ​ o ​ r ​ m ) ‖ \|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{mem})\|\gg\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c_{norm})\| . Although the same scale w w is applied, it amplifies this pre-existing disparity. Since the stability threshold is calibrated on the smaller ‖ ϵ n ​ o ​ r ​ m ‖ \|\epsilon_{norm}\| , the trajectory driven by the significantly larger ‖ ϵ m ​ e ​ m ‖ \|\epsilon_{mem}\| will inevitably exceed this threshold. Thus, the violation of the stability region is primarily driven by the sharpness of the memorized minimum (large β \beta ), which is then scaled up by w w to cross the boundary defined by normal statistics. ∎ Theorem 3 (Normal 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} Stability). Let 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)} be the reconstructed initial latent at step t t in DDIM, and let ℛ 0 ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{0}^{(t)} be the stability region in Def. 4 . Then, for normal generations, we have: 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ∈ ℛ 0 ( t ) , ∀ t ∈ { 1 , … , T } . \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\in\mathcal{R}_{0}^{(t)},\quad\forall t\in\{1,\dots,T\}. Sketch. The DDIM formulation deterministically maps 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} and ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} to 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)} . For normal prompts, ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} behaves regularly, leading to a stable and bounded reconstruction 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)} . ∎ Proof. Recall that in DDIM, the reconstructed initial latent at step t t is given by 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) = 1 α t ​ ( 𝐳 t − 1 − α t ⋅ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) ) , \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}}\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c)\right), where α t \alpha_{t} is a fixed schedule parameter and ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} is the denoising prediction. For normal prompts, the output ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) \epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) is governed by the learned distribution and is assumed to be sub-Gaussian, as in the previous theorem. Thus, for each t t , the random variable ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| is also sub-Gaussian, since it is an affine transformation of sub-Gaussian variables. Let μ 0 ( t ) \mu_{0}^{(t)} and σ 0 ( t ) \sigma_{0}^{(t)} denote the empirical mean and standard deviation of ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| over normal prompts at step t t . By the sub-Gaussian tail bound, ℙ ⁡ ( | ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ − μ 0 ( t ) | ≥ γ ​ σ 0 ( t ) ) ≤ 2 ​ exp ⁡ ( − γ 2 2 ) , \mathbb{P}\left(|\|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\|-\mu_{0}^{(t)}|\geq\gamma\sigma_{0}^{(t)}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2}\right), where γ \gamma is a positive constant. Therefore, for a sufficiently large γ \gamma (e.g., γ = 3 \gamma=3 ), the probability that ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| falls outside the interval [ μ 0 ( t ) − γ ​ σ 0 ( t ) , μ 0 ( t ) + γ ​ σ 0 ( t ) ] [\mu_{0}^{(t)}-\gamma\sigma_{0}^{(t)},\,\mu_{0}^{(t)}+\gamma\sigma_{0}^{(t)}] is exponentially small. By the union bound over all T T steps, the probability that any ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\| deviates from ℛ 0 ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{0}^{(t)} is at most 2 T exp ( − γ 2 / 2 ) 2T\exp(-\gamma^{2}/2) , which remains small for moderate T T and γ \gamma . Thus, with high probability, for all t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) ‖ ∈ ℛ 0 ( t ) = [ μ 0 ( t ) − γ ​ σ 0 ( t ) , μ 0 ( t ) + γ ​ σ 0 ( t ) ] \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}\|\in\mathcal{R}_{0}^{(t)}=[\mu_{0}^{(t)}-\gamma\sigma_{0}^{(t)},\,\mu_{0}^{(t)}+\gamma\sigma_{0}^{(t)}] as claimed. This completes the proof that reconstructed latents from non-memorized prompts tend to stay within their corresponding empirical stability region throughout the generation process in DDIM. ∎

sections.heading: Appendix B Theoretical Connections to Wen’s Metric
sections.text: Our work introduces a trajectory stability framework that unifies and extends prior empirical observations on inference guidance. Here, we clarify how our statistical boundaries theoretically relate to, yet practically transcend, the guidance magnitude metric proposed by Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . Detection: From Absolute Heuristics to Statistical Outliers. Wen et al. define their detection signal based on the magnitude of the conditional guidance term: M Wen = ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) ‖ 2 M_{\text{Wen}}=\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi)\|_{2} . In diffusion solvers, the latent update vector δ t \delta_{t} is locally proportional to this CFG output: δ t ≈ Δ ​ t ⋅ ϵ θ CFG = Δ ​ t ⋅ [ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) + w ⋅ ( ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) ) ] . \delta_{t}\approx\Delta t\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{CFG}}=\Delta t\cdot\left[\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi)+w\cdot(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi))\right]. For memorized generations, the guidance term dominates the update magnitude. Thus, we have the approximation: ‖ δ t ‖ ≈ Δ ​ t ⋅ w ⋅ ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) ‖ = C ⋅ M Wen , \|\delta_{t}\|\approx\Delta t\cdot w\cdot\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi)\|=C\cdot M_{\text{Wen}}, where C C is a scaling factor involving the step size and guidance scale. While this confirms that both our method and Wen’s track the same underlying “over-guidance” force, the detection paradigms are fundamentally different. Wen et al. treat detection as an absolute thresholding problem on M Wen M_{\text{Wen}} . Since M Wen M_{\text{Wen}} varies drastically across different timesteps and model checkpoints, finding a functional threshold is often heuristic and brittle. In contrast, we reframe detection as a distributional outlier problem. By enforcing the empirical stability region, we do not care about the absolute value of the force, but rather whether this force violates the statistical laws of natural image generation ( s t = ( ‖ δ t ‖ − μ t ) / σ t > γ s_{t}=(\|\delta_{t}\|-\mu_{t})/\sigma_{t}>\gamma ). This shift from magnitude to probability makes our method model-agnostic and time-invariant, providing a robust, calibrated standard for what constitutes an anomaly. Mitigation: Global Suppression vs. Manifold Projection. The distinction is even more critical in mitigation. Prior work typically analyzes memorization in the noise space ( ϵ \epsilon ). Our introduction of the reconstructed initial latent 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} maps these deviations into the signal space , revealing the semantic impact of memorization. Substituting the CFG formula into the definition of 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} , we obtain: 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) = 𝐳 t α ¯ t − 1 − α ¯ t α ¯ t ​ ( ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) + w ⋅ ( ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) ) ) . \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}=\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}-\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\left(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi)+w\cdot(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi))\right). Let 𝐳 ^ 0 , ϕ \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0,\phi} be the reconstruction based solely on the unconditional prediction. The deviation caused by the guidance term is: 𝐳 ^ 0 ( t ) − 𝐳 ^ 0 , ϕ = − w ​ 1 − α ¯ t α ¯ t ​ ( ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , c ) − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , ϕ ) ) . \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0,\phi}=-w\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\left(\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},c)-\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},\phi)\right). Taking the norm, we see the geometric interpretation of Wen’s metric in the image manifold: ‖ Δ ​ 𝐳 ^ 0 ‖ ∝ w ⋅ M Wen . \|\Delta\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\|\propto w\cdot M_{\text{Wen}}. This relation shows that excessive guidance pushes the estimated image 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} off the natural image manifold. Wen et al. mitigate this by suppressing the guidance signal via iterative prompt embedding optimization. Such a strategy acts as signal attenuation: they dampen the force driving the generation to avoid memorization. However, this comes with the heavy cost of optimization latency (“detect-then-retry”) and potential under- or over-mitigation from embedding modification only at the first timestep without an appropriate threshold on M Wen M_{\text{Wen}} . Our approach, conversely, performs surgical correction via on-the-fly adaptive projection throughout the entire generation process. Instead of attenuating the guidance force blindly, we allow it to remain strong as long as the trajectory is within the stability region. Only when 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} breaches the stability boundary do we intervene, clamping it specifically to the boundary of the normal distribution ( ℛ 0 ( t ) \mathcal{R}_{0}^{(t)} ). This strategy essentially retains the maximum safe guidance, preserving generation quality and semantic detail without the overhead of optimization.

sections.heading: D.1. Datasets
sections.text: • Memorized Prompts: For SD 1.4 and 1.5, we use 500 500 memorized prompts sampled from ( Webster, 2023 ) , which are also used by ( Wen et al., 2024 ) for evaluating memorization detection. For SD 2.1, we use 219 219 memorized prompts, following the setup of ( Ren et al., 2024 ) . • Non-Memorized Prompts: We follow ( Wen et al., 2024 ) to build a 500 500 prompts set from the Lexica-art gallery ( Gustavosta/Stable-Diffusion-Prompts ), the MS-COCO-2017 validation set and GPT-4 generated prompts. • Reference Prompts: We sample a total of 500 500 non-memorized prompts from the LAION-400M dataset ( Schuhmann et al., 2021 ) as reference prompts for estimating the stability regions. From these, we randomly select 50 50 prompts for all evaluation unless specified. These prompts are distinct from those used in the detection and mitigation tasks.

sections.heading: D.2. Models
sections.text: For pretrained models, we use SD 1.4 ( CompVis/stable-diffusion-v1-4 ), 1.5 ( runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5 ), and 2.1 ( stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1 ) from the HuggingFace model hub. For finetuned models, we reuse the SD 1.4 finetuned by ( Wen et al., 2024 ) open-sourced in their GitHub repository. They use 200 200 LAION data points, each duplicated 200 200 times as the memorized set, and 120,000 120,000 distinct LAION data points to retain the generalization ability of the model. The memorized set for this model is therefore the 200 200 duplicated prompts used during fine-tuning. Figure 7. PNDM generation process on SD 1.4 using strong/mild/non- memorized prompts. Figure 8. sections.heading: D.3. Metrics
sections.text: Following previous works ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) , we use the following metrics: • AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve): Measures the overall performance of the detection method over varying thresholds, implemented with scikit-learn . • TPR@ 1 % 1\% FPR (True Positive Rate at 1% False Positive Rate): Evaluates the detection performance at a low false positive rate, implemented with scikit-learn . • SSCD (Self-Supervised Copying Detection ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ) ): Evaluates the similarity between two images with a contrastive trained model. We use the sscd_disc_large model parameter provided in the GitHub repository of the original paper, in accordance with ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . • CLIP Score : Measures the semantic similarity between generated images and text prompts using CLIP embeddings. We use the openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 model from the transformers library. • FID (Fréchet Inception Distance): Evaluates the quality and diversity of generated images by comparing their distribution to real images using Inception extracted features. We use the clean-fid library to compute FID scores, which is a widely used implementation for computing FID. We evaluate CLIP score on memorized prompts and non-memorized prompts separately, and report both scores. When calculating FID, we use the LAION-400M dataset as the reference distribution, following the setting of ( Ren et al., 2024 ) . The FID is computed as the feature distribution divergence between the set of synthesized images and the reference distribution.

sections.heading: D.4. Baseline Settings
sections.text: • RTA ( Somepalli et al., 2023 ) : Following the implementation in ( Wen et al., 2024 ) , we randomly add four tokens for each prompt using the pipeline’s tokenizer. • Ren et al. ( Ren et al., 2024 ) : For detection, we adopt the pipeline from the official open-source implementation. For each sample, we record the attention entropy at every step of the denoising process and then compute a final detection score using the metric D D proposed in the original paper. For mitigation, we scale or mask the attention scores of the begin and summary tokens within the cross-attention layers following the hyperparameters in the open-source code. • Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) : We also utilize the official pipeline for this baseline. For detection, the guidance magnitude at each denoising step is saved as the score. For multi-step detection, we follow the source code’s approach by averaging the scores from all preceding steps to obtain the final score. For mitigation, we optimize for 10 10 steps at the first step of the denoising process, with l t ​ a ​ r ​ g ​ e ​ t = 3 l_{target}=3 according to the settings in the open-source code. • Jeon et al. ( Jeon et al., 2025 ) : We use the official open-source code provided by the authors. For detection, we only expand the detection timesteps to the first 3 3 steps since the computational cost of this method is very high. Note that the original paper only performs detection at the first step, which should lead to slightly worse detection performance. For mitigation, we follow the default settings with an optimization threshold of 8.2 8.2 and a maximum of 10 10 iterations. • Jain et al. ( Jain et al., 2025 ) : We dynamically find the first local minimum of the latent update to use as the “transition point” following the implementation in the open-source code, and take the negative of the guidance scale before the transition point, i.e., the Opposite-Guidance setting. For all baselines and our proposed method, we set the number of inference steps to 50 50 and the guidance scale to 7.5 7.5 following the settings of all these baselines. For detection, we conduct evaluations under three distinct settings: a single seed ( 0 0 ), four seeds ( 0 − 3 0-3 ), and eight seeds ( 0 − 7 0-7 ). In the multi-seed settings, the final scores are calculated by averaging the results from each individual seed. For mitigation, to simulate a real-world scenario, we apply a “detect-then-mitigate” strategy to the baselines that offer a detection mechanism. The threshold is set to achieve a 1 % 1\% false positive rate on LAION-400M reference prompts. For mitigation, we uniformly use the DDIM scheduler and report the results from a fixed random seed 0 0 .

sections.heading: D.5. Implementation Details
sections.text: Our method consists of two main components: memorization detection and memorization mitigation. We mainly rely on the callback_on_step_end feature of the Stable Diffusion pipeline to implement our method. To estimate the empirical stability regions, we record the latent representations and the denoising predictions at each step during the diffusion process. Then, for detection, we take the latent representations at each step and compute the distances (Z-scores) to the stability regions. For mitigation, after each denoising step, we check if the current latent representation is within the stability region. If not, we estimate 𝐳 0 ( t ) \mathbf{z}_{0}^{(t)} with the current latent representation 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} and the denoising prediction ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , c ) \epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,c) , and then we perform the mitigation in Algorithm 2 . The resulting latent replaces the original latent when the callback returns. For hyperparameters, the thresholds τ mild \tau_{\text{mild}} and τ strong \tau_{\text{strong}} are empirically determined based on the statistical distribution of Z-scores from normal prompts. We set τ mild = 3 \tau_{\text{mild}}=3 and τ strong = 14 \tau_{\text{strong}}=14 , which correspond to the 99.7 % 99.7\% and extreme outlier regions under a sub-Gaussian assumption. These values are validated to achieve robust detection and mitigation performance across multiple models and datasets in our experiments. The mild mitigation steps k k is set to 10 10 , based on empirical analysis of the typical duration of instability in memorized generations with mitigation applied. Previous works ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) have made similar claims that this range is effective for mitigating memorization artifacts without significantly degrading image quality. sections.heading: E.1. Degraded Generations with Memorized Prompts
sections.text: To further elucidate our finding that memorized prompts lead to degraded generation, we present additional degradation examples. In Fig. 7 , we illustrate the PNDM generation process for strong, mild and non-memorized prompts, represented in red, orange, and green, respectively. For memorized prompts, degradation occurs throughout the entire denoising process, whereas the generation quality for non-memorized prompts remains normal. As can be seen, both the latent norm and latent update norm for memorized prompts deviate from the stability region. This deviation is more pronounced in the latter, demonstrating that our proposed detection metric provides a strong signal for identifying memorization. In Fig. 8 , we present the generation results for the same prompts using the DDIM scheduler. Although the final images generated by DDIM do not exhibit degradation, the intermediate results suffer from degradation because the latent norm and latent update norm temporarily deviate from the stability region during the process. This example illustrates that the latent update can be used as a general signal for detecting memorization, even when the final image quality is not degraded.

sections.heading: E.2. Distribution and Scale of Reference Prompts
sections.text: To investigate whether detection performance depends on the distribution of reference prompts, we analyze the norm distributions during inference using reference prompts from various data sources, as shown in Fig. 9 . We observe that the distributions of both 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} and δ t \delta_{t} norms span similar ranges across different sources, indicating that our method is robust to the choice of reference prompts. Among these sources, we select prompts from LAION-400M, as it is the training set for SD and thus most accessible to model providers in practice. Furthermore, varying the scale of reference prompts also yields similar norm distributions, as illustrated in Fig. 10 . We further evaluate detection performance with different numbers of reference prompts in Fig. 11 and 12 . The results demonstrate that a moderate number of prompts is sufficient to achieve strong detection performance. To balance detection accuracy and computational cost, we use 50 50 reference prompts in all experiments. Figure 9. Similar stability regions by prompts from different non-memorized datasets. sections.heading: E.4. Memorization Mitigation on Pretrained SD 1.4 and Finetuned SD 1.4
sections.text: Table 7 and 8 present the mitigation results on pretrained SD 1.4 and finetuned SD 1.4, respectively. From Table 8 , we show that our method effectively mitigates memorization artifacts in the finetuned SD 1.4 model, while maintaining high image quality and semantic alignment. Note that the memorization induced by finetuning is less stronger than that in pretrained models. Baselines still struggle to mitigate memorization because they fail to detect memorization accurately when memorized generations become hard to recognize in this setting. Jeon et al. achieve decent performance in this setting, likely because the weaker memorization induced by finetuning is more easily mitigated by their local curvature-aware optimization. In addition, we point out that previous research usually does not consider the realistic detect-and-mitigate scenario in our work. Instead, they apply mitigation to all generations without detection in advance. Therefore, they may exhibit an illusion of mitigation effectiveness. Table 7. sections.heading: E.5. More Case Studies
sections.text: Fig. 13 presents additional generation cases, further validating the effectiveness of our method in various scenarios. Compared to the baselines, the baseline generations are quickly drawn towards memorized content in the early steps, resulting in obvious memorization artifacts. In contrast, our method detects and adaptively mitigates memorization at each step, ultimately producing images without memorized content. These cases further demonstrate the necessity of on-the-fly detection and stepwise mitigation for preventing memorization in diffusion models.
